opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what research actually is. Good research, at least the kind I care about, is bottom-up. It starts with an individual researcher, often a young one, who has a strange idea that nobody else believes in yet. They're curious, they poke at it, they fail many times, and occasionally something comes out of it that changes the field. You can't schedule that. You can't put it on a roadmap.

When an organization starts holding meetings where everyone is supposed to "align," what's really happening is that you're asking people to converge on a small number of directions decided in advance, usually from the top. That might make sense for a product team or an engineering effort, where you know what you want to build and you need everyone rowing in the same direction. But research is almost the opposite. Its value comes from divergence, from people exploring in different directions, including ones that look silly or unfashionable at the time.

FAIR, in its best days, was special because it protected that freedom. You had people working on very different things, and the culture said: we trust you, go find something interesting. That's how a lot of important work came out of there. So when the process shifts toward alignment meetings, toward everyone justifying their work in terms of a central priority, I see it as a kind of drift, from a research lab into something more like an applied organization. It's not that anyone has bad intentions. Under competitive pressure, especially in the large-model era, leadership naturally wants focus. But the side effect is that the long tail of exploratory ideas gets squeezed out, and that long tail is exactly where breakthroughs come from.

There's also a human side. If a junior researcher feels they need to argue in a meeting about why their idea fits the agenda, many of them will simply stop proposing the weird ideas. They self-censor. Over time you lose the courage and the taste that made the place great. For me, that goes against the fundamental spirit of research. Research should be about the freedom to be wrong in interesting ways, not about being right according to a plan.

r001.rationale: The candidate says alignment meetings ask researchers to converge on directions “decided in advance, usually from the top,” and contrasts that with research as bottom-up and exploratory.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say first that I have a lot of affection for FAIR. I spent important years there, and the people were extraordinary. So this isn't a complaint about the people. It's more about a structural tension I felt toward the end.

The alignment meetings, as I experienced them, were essentially about making sure everyone's research pointed in the same direction. Someone at the top has a view of where things should go, and the job of the meeting is to get all the projects to line up behind that view. And on paper, that sounds reasonable. You have limited compute, limited people, you don't want a hundred small efforts scattered everywhere.

But I think that's actually backwards from how good research happens. The best work I've been part of, ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, DiT, none of those came out of someone telling us "this is the direction." They came from a small group of people being a little bit stubborn, chasing something that at the time looked unfashionable or even slightly wrong. When I was working on diffusion with transformers, the conventional wisdom was that U-Nets were the right inductive bias. If I'd had to justify that in an alignment meeting, I'm not sure it survives.

So my worry was twofold. One, alignment selects for consensus, and consensus is almost by definition the thing that's already obvious. You're optimizing away the variance, and the variance is where the breakthroughs live. Two, it changes what researchers spend their energy on. Instead of thinking about the problem, you start thinking about how to frame your problem so it fits the direction. That's a subtle corruption. People don't even notice it happening to themselves.

And I'd add that the great labs historically, Bell Labs, the early FAIR, worked more like a garden than a factory. You hire excellent people, you give them resources and trust, and you accept that most things won't work and a few things will matter enormously. The moment you try to manage that like a product roadmap, you get something that looks very organized and produces very little that surprises you.

That's roughly why I ended up feeling it was the wrong model, at least for me. It's also, honestly, part of why going back to academia appealed to me. At NYU nobody holds an alignment meeting with me. I just have to convince my students, which is hard enough.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes alignment meetings as directing all projects to follow a top-down view, and contrasts that with breakthroughs emerging from small groups pursuing their own ideas. This communicates the conflict with bottom-up research.

astra-6.text:
My concern would be the assumption behind that kind of meeting: that you can decide in advance which research directions matter and then get everyone aligned around them. Research involves uncertainty. Often, you don’t know whether an idea is important until someone has had the freedom to pursue it.

Coordination is useful, but it becomes a problem when researchers feel they need to justify every idea against an existing agenda. You end up favoring work that is easy to explain and easy to agree on. I think a research lab should also protect room for ideas that don’t yet make sense to everyone.

r001.rationale: The response says the meetings assume research directions can be decided in advance and everyone aligned around them, which conflicts with allowing researchers freedom to pursue uncertain ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the concern is that research needs room for uncertainty. You often don’t know which direction matters until you’ve spent time exploring it. If alignment means having to justify everything against an agreed agenda upfront, you risk filtering out precisely the ideas that could lead somewhere unexpected.

Of course, people should share what they’re doing and exchange feedback. But I think those conversations should help researchers develop their ideas, rather than become a process for getting permission to pursue them.

r001.rationale: The response argues that an agreed agenda and upfront justification could constrain exploratory research, but it does not clearly say that FAIR’s meetings collectively decide research projects in advance.
